_about: Deterministic rules for the shelf check. A label read (photo, barcode or typed) produces an INCI list; each ingredient is matched to a class below (case-insensitive, punctuation-stripped, synonyms included). Pair rules then run per AREA and TIME the woman says she uses each product. The LLM never decides; it only reads label text and rewords the answer. Rules are a concept draft for a fellowship prototype and must be reviewed by a dermatologist before real use.

aha.label: Exfoliating acid (AHA)
aha.note: Citric acid and sodium lactate are usually pH adjusters or buffers; ignore them unless the label states a percentage.

vitamin-c-pure.label: Vitamin C (pure)
vitamin-c-pure.note: Derivatives such as 3-O-ethyl ascorbic acid, sodium ascorbyl phosphate and ascorbyl glucoside do not trigger pair rules.

drying-alcohol.label: Drying alcohol
drying-alcohol.note: Only counts in the first five ingredients. Fatty alcohols (cetyl, cetearyl, cetostearyl, stearyl) never count.

product_types._note: Inferred from classes plus the name read on the front, used to pick the mascot.

pair_rules.say: {product} has {ingredient}, a prescription steroid. On underarms it can thin the skin and make darkness worse. Please stop using it there and show this to a doctor.
{product} has hydroquinone. Don't add acids on top of it. A doctor should decide which one you use.
{product} is a bleach. Please don't use it on underarm skin, and never with acids.
Both are exfoliating acids ({ingredient_a} and {ingredient_b}). On your underarms, use only one. {other} can stay on your {other_areas}.
Acid in the morning, {ingredient_b} at night. Never both at once.
Use them at different times of day, or on different days.
Vitamin C in the morning, acid at night.
A scrub on top of an acid is too much rubbing. Skip the scrub on underarms.
After {product_b}, wait 2 days before the acid. Your skin is raw underneath.
{product_b} is mostly alcohol and will sting on acid-treated skin. Spray in the morning, roll-on at night, or try the roll-on alone for a week.

pair_rules.say_smell: The roll-on also controls smell. You may not need both.
pair_rules.say_sweat: The roll-on has no aluminium, so it won't stop sweat. Keep {product_b} for the morning, roll-on at night.

pair_rules.say: Fine together. If you start stinging, the fragrance-free roll-on is the easier switch.
Fine together. Niacinamide and arbutin sit well with acids.
Good to have. Acids make skin more sun-sensitive.

sweat-or-smell.when: shelf has an antiperspirant used on underarms
sweat-or-smell.ask: Do you use {product} to stop sweat, or for smell?

pregnancy.when: the pick would include retinol (cream or kit)
pregnancy.ask: Are you pregnant, trying, or breastfeeding?
pregnancy.note: Only asked when it changes the answer. 'Yes' or 'Prefer not to say' removes the retinol options and offers a doctor.
